chapter_title: Basic Input/Output and Control Flow (Part 1: Conditional Statements)

screens.title: Basic I/O and Conditional Statements
screens.subtitle: Using printf and scanf to interact with users, then making decisions with if / else

narration.text: In this lesson we open programs to real users. You'll learn how to print formatted output and read keyboard input, how the address-of operator connects scanf to variables, and how conditional statements let your program choose different actions. We start with the print function to format messages and numbers so users understand results. Then we make input work reliably by using the correct format specifiers and by passing memory addresses. Finally, we explore conditional flow: a single if, chains of else if, nested decisions, and the compact ternary form. You will see concrete examples: printing a greeting with a name and numeric formatting, reading an integer score safely, and a grade calculator that maps numeric ranges to letter grades. I'll point out common pitfalls you should avoid, such as missing the ampersand when using scanf, buffer and string size issues, stray newline characters affecting character reads, and misplaced curly braces that break program logic. By the end you'll understand not only the A P I calls but also the reasoning behind format specifiers, input validation basics, and why curly braces matter for correctness. Think about how these primitives let your programs become interactive — what small program will you write first that asks a user a question and responds differently based on their answer?

keyIdea.title: Interactive programs start here
keyIdea.text: Mastering formatted output, safe input, and structured conditionals lets you build programs that respond to users and make decisions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Introduction

Basic I/O & Control Flow

In this chapter you will learn to format output, read input safely, and control program flow with conditionals.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Why I/O matters

Programs talk to users through formatted text and react to typed input; that opens them to real-world tasks like calculators, quizzes, and utilities.

Why conditionals matter

Conditionals let your program branch based on input and state, enabling different behavior for different users or data ranges.

What we'll cover
  • Formatted printing with printf and common format specifiers.
  • Reading input with scanf, the address-of operator, and safety notes.
  • Conditional constructs: if, else if, else, nested if, and the ternary operator.
Visual Concept
Keyboard → scanf() → variable memory (address)
printf() formats values → Console output
if / else → choose which message to print
Explore Key Topics
Formatted Output — control decimals and width with format specifiers
Safe Input — always pass addresses to scanf and watch buffer sizes
Conditional Logic — chains and nesting decide program flow

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain and why they matter

narration.text: These objectives prepare you to read and write console data and to make decisions in your programs. First, you'll learn to use the print function to create clear, formatted messages. Clear formatting helps users read numbers and text and helps you debug. Second, you'll learn to use the scan function to accept different data types from the keyboard; that includes understanding how format specifiers map to types and why you must pass the variable's address. Third, you'll practice choosing the correct format specifier for integers, floating point, characters, and strings so data doesn't get misinterpreted. Finally, you'll implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else so your program reacts differently based on user input. Each objective includes a short competency milestone you can verify with a simple program. Together these skills let you build small interactive programs like calculators, quizzes, and validators. As you work, notice the safety patterns: checking input success, guarding string sizes, and always using braces to avoid subtle bugs. Which objective feels most unfamiliar now, and where will you focus first?

keyIdea.title: What you'll be able to do
keyIdea.text: Format output, read typed input safely, select correct format specifiers, and build conditional logic to branch program behavior.

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on safe habits and verification. You will learn two safety checks: always pass addresses for non-array variables when using the scan function, and be mindful of buffer sizes when reading strings. Missing the address-of operator is a common runtime error that you can avoid by treating scan like a function that writes to memory locations. For strings, we'll recommend using a maximum width in the format or prefer other input functions when buffers are small. You will also practice checking scan's return value to detect mismatched types early. For conditionals, adopt the habit of always using curly braces; this prevents errors where unexpected statements run unconditionally and can cause logic bugs or compilation errors. Finally, apply these practices in a small grade calculator program. The practice milestone is to write, compile, and run a program that reads a score, validates the range, and prints a correct letter grade. Safety-first habits save hours when you begin mixing inputs and character reads later.

keyIdea.title: Practice safe input
keyIdea.text: Use address-of for variables, set string width or use safer input functions, check scanf returns, and always use curly braces to maintain correct program flow.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Safety & Practice
Safety checklist
  • Always pass &variable to scanf for non-array variables so input is written into your variable's memory.
  • When using %s, limit width: use %9s for a 10-byte buffer to leave space for the null terminator.
  • Check scanf's return value; it tells how many items were successfully read.
  • Consume leftover newline characters before reading a char using scanf(" %c", &ch) or using getchar loops.
  • Always use { } even for single-line if blocks to avoid misplaced else and readability problems.
Quick mnemonic
Ampersand → Address. Braces → Block. Return value → Verify.
Try this in the shell: compile small programs and test invalid inputs to see how scanf behaves; observing failure helps you understand why checks matter.

screens.title: printf() — formatted output
screens.subtitle: Format strings, specifiers, precision, and field width

narration.text: The print function is your primary tool for communicating with users and debugging. It accepts a format string and zero or more values which replace format placeholders. Each format specifier tells the function how to format a value: %d for integers, %f for floating point, %c for characters, and %s for strings. Precision and field width let you control how numbers appear; for example, specifying two decimal places makes monetary values readable. A common pattern is combining text and specifiers to produce clear messages. For example, printing a name and score with two decimals demonstrates text plus formatted numbers. Be careful about using the correct specifier: using %f for an integer or %d for a float causes incorrect output or undefined behavior. Also remember to escape literal percent signs by using double percent. A good debugging habit is to format intermediate values so you can see exact types and ranges during development. Practice by writing small statements that print different types and by changing precision to observe rounding. Which numeric display style would you choose for a temperature reading versus a price? That choice affects user understanding.

keyIdea.title: printf guides user-facing output
keyIdea.text: Use format specifiers and precision to present values clearly and to aid debugging.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › printf()
Code examples (try these in a C file)
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int score = 95;
  double price = 12.5;
  printf("Hello, %s! Your score is %d.
", "Alice", score);
  printf("Price: $%.2f
", price);
  printf("Literal percent: 50%% complete
");
  return 0;
}
Explanation & tips
  • %d prints integers; use %i interchangeably for decimal integers.
  • Use %.2f to show two decimal places for floats or doubles when printing money or precise values.
  • %s expects a null-terminated character array; do not pass non-string pointers or uninitialized arrays.
  • To print a percent sign, include %% in the format string.
Key Takeaway

Match specifiers to types and use precision to communicate values correctly to users.

screens.title: Format Specifiers — Common types
screens.subtitle: Choose the right placeholder for reliable I/O

narration.text: Format specifiers are the contract between your values and the print and scan functions. The most common ones you will use are %d or %i for integers, %f for floating point when printing, and %lf for double when reading with scan. Characters use %c and strings use %s. There are also specifiers for unsigned integers and size types like %u and %zu. Mismatched specifiers are a frequent source of confusing output and undefined behavior, because the function interprets the bytes you pass according to the specifier. For example, printing a double with %d will interpret the double's bytes as an integer and produce nonsense. When using scan for doubles, prefer %lf, because on some systems %f expects a float pointer and %lf expects a double pointer. A practical rule: choose the specifier that matches the variable's declared type, and when in doubt consult the variable declaration. To practice, write short examples that print the same variable with different specifiers and observe the results. This concrete contrast helps reinforce why accurate mapping matters. Format Specifiers — Common types means always map specifiers to variable types: %d/%i → int, %f → float/double for printing, %lf → double in scanf, %c → char, %s → string.. In practical terms, choose the right placeholder for reliable i/o. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Specifier ↔ Type mapping
keyIdea.text: Always map specifiers to variable types: %d/%i → int, %f → float/double for printing, %lf → double in scanf, %c → char, %s → string.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Format Specifiers
Specifier comparison
Integers
%d or %i → int
Floating point
%f → float/double for printf. Use %lf with scanf for double.
Character
%c → char (use a leading space in scanf to skip whitespace: " %c")
Strings
%s → char array; supply a max width like %9s to avoid overflow.
Practical tip

If your program prints garbage or crashes, the first check is whether the format specifier matches the variable type passed. A mismatched pair often explains strange output or runtime errors.

Mini exercise
int n = 42;
printf("as int: %d
", n);
printf("mistake as float: %f
", n);
Run this to observe the wrong output and understand why mapping matters.

screens.title: scanf() and the Address-of Operator
screens.subtitle: How scanf writes into your variables using &

narration.text: The scan function reads values from standard input and writes them into variables you supply. To do that, it needs the variable's memory location. The address-of operator provides that location. For non-array variables you must pass &variable so scanf knows where to store the value. Forgetting the ampersand is a very common beginner mistake that can crash your program or produce undefined behavior. Arrays and strings behave differently: passing the array name is already an address, so you do not use & for char name[] when reading a string with %s. Another practical detail: when reading multiple values in one call, scanf expects whitespace between them — spaces, tabs, or newlines — so typing values separated by spaces works. Always prefer checking scanf's return value; it returns the number of successfully read items, which helps detect type mismatches. Practically, write small tests: declare an int, prompt the user, call scanf("%d", &n), and then print n. That simple loop teaches the address concept and the function's contract. Ask yourself: what will happen if the input does not match the expected type?

keyIdea.title: scanf must receive addresses
keyIdea.text: Pass &variable for scalars; for arrays pass the array name. Check scanf's return value to confirm successful reads.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › scanf() & Address
Example: read an integer
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int age;
  printf("Enter your age: ");
  if (scanf("%d", &age) != 1) {
    printf("Invalid input.
");
    return 1;
  }
  printf("You entered: %d
", age);
  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • The ampersand gives scanf the variable's memory address so it can write the input value there.
  • Arrays decay to pointers, so for char name[10] you call scanf("%9s", name) without & because name already refers to an address.
  • Always check the return value to verify that scanf read the expected number of items.
Common mistake

Omitting & for scalars is a runtime error; test simple reads to internalize the address rule.

screens.title: Common scanf() Pitfalls and Mitigations
screens.subtitle: Buffer sizes, trailing newlines, and input mismatches

narration.text: scanf is simple but can surprise you if you don't account for how input is buffered and parsed. One frequent issue is buffer overflow when using %s: scanf does not know your array size and will happily write past bounds if the user types a long string. Mitigate this by specifying a width in the format, like %9s for a ten-byte array, or by using safer functions when available. Another issue is leftover newline characters. When you read numbers, the newline remains in the input stream and will be consumed by a subsequent %c read unless you handle whitespace explicitly; using a space before %c in the format string tells scanf to skip whitespace. Input mismatch is another common pitfall: if the user types non-numeric characters while scanf expects a number, scanf returns 0 and leaves that invalid input in the buffer. A practical mitigation is to check scanf's return value and clear the buffer afterward by reading characters until newline. While buffer clearing is an advanced detail we'll cover later, the habit of checking scanf's return value immediately will save you from many loops and strange behavior. These safety practices help you build robust interactive programs as you progress.

keyIdea.title: Treat scanf defensively
keyIdea.text: Specify widths for strings, consume stray newlines, and always check the return value to handle input mismatches gracefully.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › scanf() Pitfalls
Buffer overflow example
char name[10];
// Unsafe:
// scanf("%s", name);
// Safer with width:
scanf("%9s", name);
Always leave space for the null terminator and restrict input width for fixed buffers.
Trailing newline and char reads
After reading a number, the newline stays in the buffer. Use a leading space in the format: scanf(" %c", &ch) to skip whitespace, including newlines, before reading a character.
Input mismatch

If scanf expects a number and receives letters, it returns 0 and leaves the invalid input in the buffer. Check the return value to detect this case early.

screens.title: The if Statement
screens.subtitle: Making a program take one action when a condition is true

narration.text: An if statement lets your program run a block of code only when a condition evaluates to true. In C, any nonzero value is treated as true and zero as false. The condition is an expression that can use comparison operators like greater-than, less-than, and equality. A simple example is checking whether a score is at least a passing threshold and printing a message if so. Importantly, the syntax requires parentheses around the condition and braces around blocks if you want more than one statement to run. Omitting braces is legal for single statements but leads to subtle bugs; a common exam question demonstrates that a stray printf after an if without braces runs unconditionally. As a habit, always use braces to avoid confusion and to make future edits safer. Also remember you can combine logical operators such as AND and OR to form compound conditions. Practice by writing if statements that check numeric ranges or boolean flags. How would you test an if that should only run when two conditions are true? The if Statement means use if to execute code only when a condition is true; always prefer braces to avoid errors and improve clarity.. In practical terms, making a program take one action when a condition is true. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: If controls single-branch flow
keyIdea.text: Use if to execute code only when a condition is true; always prefer braces to avoid errors and improve clarity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › if Statement
Syntax example
if (score >= 60) {
  printf("You passed!
");
}
The condition must evaluate to nonzero for the block to run. Use braces to include multiple statements safely.
Common mistake demo
if (x > 5)
  printf("A
");
  printf("B
");
// The second printf always runs; use braces to fix.
Pro tip

Always add braces. It prevents logical mistakes when adding statements later.

screens.title: else if Chains and Evaluation Order
screens.subtitle: Check multiple conditions in sequence without redundant checks

narration.text: When you need to choose from many alternatives, an else if chain tests conditions in order until one is true. The first true condition's block runs and the rest are skipped. This makes ordering important: place the most specific or highest-priority checks first. For example, mapping numeric scores to letter grades uses descending thresholds: test for 90 or above first, then 80 or above, and so on, so a score of 92 matches the A condition and stops. A common misconception is that separate if statements are equivalent to an else if chain; they are not. Separate ifs will all be evaluated independently and may produce multiple matching outputs, while an else if chain guarantees only a single match. Use else as a final catch-all when none of the earlier conditions apply. When performance matters and checks are expensive, an ordered chain avoids unnecessary evaluations. Practice by writing a grade mapping and testing edge values like 89, 90, and 100 to confirm the chain behaves as intended. else if Chains and Evaluation Order means an else if chain stops at the first true condition — design the order so the right case matches earliest.. In practical terms, check multiple conditions in sequence without redundant checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Order matters in else if chains
keyIdea.text: An else if chain stops at the first true condition — design the order so the right case matches earliest.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › else if Chains
Grade mapping example
if (score < 0 || score > 100) {
  printf("Error
");
} else if (score >= 90) {
  printf("Grade: A
");
} else if (score >= 80) {
  printf("Grade: B
");
} else if (score >= 70) {
  printf("Grade: C
");
} else if (score >= 60) {
  printf("Grade: D
");
} else {
  printf("Grade: F
");
}
Key points
  • The chain evaluates top to bottom and stops at the first true branch.
  • Order thresholds from most specific (highest) to least to prevent accidental matches.
  • Use an else as the final catch-all for unexpected values.

screens.title: Nested if and Logical Operators
screens.subtitle: Express compound logic and avoid deep nesting when possible

narration.text: Nested if statements let you check a condition and, inside its true branch, check another condition. This supports multi-level decisions, such as passing a logged-in check before testing admin privileges. While nesting is expressive, too many levels make code hard to read and maintain. Often you can combine conditions with logical AND and OR operators to flatten the structure: use && to require both conditions, and || to allow either. For example, instead of nesting an if for user_logged_in and then an if for user_is_admin, you can write if (user_logged_in && user_is_admin). But be mindful of short-circuiting: with && the second operand is evaluated only if the first is true; with || the second is evaluated only if the first is false. This can be useful to avoid evaluating expensive expressions unless needed. When nesting, prefer early returns to reduce indentation. Always use braces for clarity. Practice rewriting nested logic using combined conditions and compare readability and behavior. Nested if and Logical Operators means use logical operators to avoid deep nesting; remember short-circuit behavior for performance and safety.. In practical terms, express compound logic and avoid deep nesting when possible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer clear compound checks
keyIdea.text: Use logical operators to avoid deep nesting; remember short-circuit behavior for performance and safety.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Nested if & Operators
Nested example
if (user_logged_in) {
  if (user_is_admin) {
    printf("Welcome, Admin!
");
  } else {
    printf("Welcome, User!
");
  }
}
Flattened with logical AND
if (user_logged_in && user_is_admin) {
  printf("Welcome, Admin!
");
} else if (user_logged_in) {
  printf("Welcome, User!
");
} else {
  printf("Please log in.
");
}
Flattening reduces indentation and often improves clarity; ensure expressions are safe when short-circuiting is relied upon.

screens.title: Hands-on: Grade Calculator Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Build a CLI program that reads a score and prints a letter grade

narration.text: Let's walk through a complete small program that links input, validation, and conditional branching. The program prompts for an integer score, uses scanf to read it into a variable, checks that scanf succeeded, clears the input buffer if necessary, validates the numeric range, and then uses an else if chain to map the score to a letter grade. After the conditional chain it demonstrates the ternary operator to compute a pass/fail status concisely. This walkthrough shows how the pieces integrate: format specifiers make the prompt readable, the address-of operator allows scanf to write into the score variable, return-value checking guards against invalid input, and a well-ordered else if chain ensures the correct grade is selected. Try compiling and running the program with edge cases like -5, 100, and non-numeric input to observe behavior and to practice defensive checks. As you type and test, notice how placing the range check before grade mapping prevents invalid values from producing a misleading grade. What small improvement could you add next to make input handling more robust? Hands-on: Grade Calculator Walkthrough means a complete interactive program validates input, maps values through conditional chains, and reports results clearly to the user.. In practical terms, build a cli program that reads a score and prints a letter grade. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Combine I/O and conditionals
keyIdea.text: A complete interactive program validates input, maps values through conditional chains, and reports results clearly to the user.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Grade Calculator
Source file: grade_calculator.c
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int score;
  printf("--- Grade Calculator ---
");
  printf("Enter the student's numerical score (0-100): ");
  if (scanf("%d", &score) != 1) {
    printf("Invalid input. Please enter a number.
");
    return 1;
  }
  while (getchar() != '
' && !feof(stdin));

  if (score < 0 || score > 100) {
    printf("Error: Score must be between 0 and 100.
");
  } else if (score >= 90) {
    printf("Grade: A
");
  } else if (score >= 80) {
    printf("Grade: B
");
  } else if (score >= 70) {
    printf("Grade: C
");
  } else if (score >= 60) {
    printf("Grade: D
");
  } else {
    printf("Grade: F
");
  }

  const char* status = (score >= 60 && score <= 100) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
  printf("Overall Status: %s
", status);
  return 0;
}
Walkthrough highlights
  • Check scanf's return value to detect non-numeric input and abort or reprompt.
  • Clear leftover input so future reads behave predictably.
  • Validate ranges before mapping to grades to avoid misleading results for out-of-range numbers.
  • Use the ternary operator for short conditional assignments like pass/fail status.
Try cases: 95, 82, 70, 55, -5, 105, and a non-number to observe behaviors and error messages.

screens.title: Ternary Operator and Concise Conditionals
screens.subtitle: A compact form for simple conditional assignments

narration.text: The ternary operator provides a concise way to select between two expressions based on a condition. Written as condition? expression_if_true : expression_if_false, it evaluates the condition and yields one of the two expressions. It's ideal for simple assignments or passing short conditional values to print functions. For example, you can compute a pass/fail string from a numeric score with a single line rather than a multi-line if-else. While compact, overuse can make code hard to read, especially when nested ternaries are used. Prefer ternary for short, clear choices and fall back to full if-else for complex logic. Ternary expressions are expressions, not statements, so they can be used where a value is expected. Practice converting small if-else assignments into ternary expressions and then decide which form is clearer. The guiding rule is clarity: choose the form that a future reader will understand fastest. Ternary Operator and Concise Conditionals means use condition ? value1 : value2 for brief conditional assignments, keeping readability as the priority.. In practical terms, a compact form for simple conditional assignments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ternary for short choices
keyIdea.text: Use condition ? value1 : value2 for brief conditional assignments, keeping readability as the priority.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Ternary Operator
Ternary example
const char* status = (score >= 60 && score <= 100) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
printf("Overall Status: %s
", status);
The ternary returns one of the two string literals based on the condition, making the code compact and expressive for simple choices.
When not to use it

Avoid nested ternaries and long expressions inside the ternary; prefer a clear if-else when the logic involves multiple steps or side effects.

Check your clarity

If the ternary requires comments to explain, rewrite it as a short if-else.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points. First, the print function formats output using specifiers and precision; match specifiers to types to avoid incorrect output. Second, the scan function reads input into memory addresses — use the address-of operator for scalars and restrict string widths to avoid buffer overflow. Third, always check scanf's return value to detect mismatched input and consider clearing the input buffer when needed. Fourth, conditional statements let programs branch: if runs when a condition is true, else if chains evaluate in order and else provides a catch-all. Finally, use curly braces to avoid misplaced-else bugs and prefer logical operators to flatten nested ifs when it improves clarity. Keep practice focused: write small programs, test edge cases, and read compiler warnings. These foundations make your programs interactive, predictable, and easier to debug.

screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders for safe, clear code

narration.text: Wrap up with three concise reminders: first, always match format specifiers to variable types to avoid incorrect output or undefined behavior. Second, when using scanf for scalars, pass the address-of the variable; for strings, restrict width or choose safer input functions when buffers are limited. Third, structure conditionals thoughtfully: order else if branches from most specific to least, always use curly braces, and prefer simple ternary expressions only for very short assignments. These habits will make your programs easier to test, debug, and extend.
